passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — peremptory norms from which no derogation is permitted under international law — occupies an unresolved position at the intersection of customary international law and treaty regimes. Unlike ordinary customary norms, which may be displaced by subsequent treaty obligations between consenting states, a jus cogens norm is, in the language of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, one "accepted and recognized by the international community of states as a whole as a norm from which no derogation is permitted." The Convention further provides that any treaty conflicting with such a norm is void ab initio. Yet the Convention does not identify which specific norms qualify for this status, leaving that determination to a process whose doctrinal foundations remain deeply contested.

The principal difficulty is one of circular validation. A jus cogens norm is said to derive its peremptory character from the acceptance of the international community as a whole, but the machinery for registering that acceptance — decisions of international tribunals, state practice, opinio juris — is the same machinery used to establish ordinary customary norms. Critics, drawing on legal-positivist premises, have argued that this circularity renders jus cogens analytically indistinguishable from elevated custom: if a norm achieves peremptory status through the same evidentiary process as ordinary custom, no meaningful hierarchy exists between them. Defenders of the doctrine respond that the threshold is qualitatively, not merely quantitatively, different — that peremptory norms reflect a near-universal moral consensus so fundamental that no bilateral agreement ought to be capable of abrogating them. The International Court of Justice, in its 1998 advisory opinion on reservations to the Convention Against Torture, appeared to endorse the defenders' position, characterizing jus cogens norms as obligations erga omnes whose binding force is independent of reciprocity. However, the Court offered no satisfactory account of why the same consensual validation process should yield two categorically distinct classes of norm.

A related complication arises when jus cogens intersects with the principle of lex specialis — the rule that a more specific legal regime governs over a more general one where the two conflict. States have, on occasion, argued before international arbitral panels that a bilateral investment treaty constitutes lex specialis capable of displacing the more general prohibition against expropriation without compensation, itself sometimes asserted to be a jus cogens norm. Arbitral tribunals have been divided in their treatment of this argument; some have accepted that lex specialis can modulate the application of jus cogens in narrow commercial contexts, while others have treated such arguments as categorically impermissible on the ground that peremptory norms admit of no displacement whatsoever, including by specific treaty regime. The latter position is logically more consistent with the Vienna Convention's text, but it leaves arbitral panels ill-equipped to manage the significant volume of investment disputes in which compensation standards are genuinely contested.

Regrettably, neither the Court's advisory opinions nor the work of the International Law Commission's 2019 draft conclusions on jus cogens has resolved these tensions in a way that international tribunals can reliably apply. One might hope that a future multilateral treaty would enumerate specific peremptory norms and establish a standing adjudicative body to determine their interaction with lex specialis claims; in the absence of such an instrument, the doctrine will remain conceptually powerful but practically unstable.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties established jus cogens as the highest class of international legal norm, but failed to identify which norms qualify for that status, thereby provoking unnecessary litigation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although jus cogens norms occupy a theoretically superior position in the hierarchy of international law, foundational ambiguities in their validation and interaction with competing principles render the doctrine practically unreliable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Legal positivists have convincingly demonstrated that jus cogens norms are analytically indistinguishable from elevated customary international law norms and therefore serve no useful doctrinal function.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The International Court of Justice's 1998 advisory opinion on reservations to the Convention Against Torture provided the most authoritative resolution of the tension between jus cogens and lex specialis.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proliferation of bilateral investment treaties has undermined the coherence of jus cogens by inviting arbitral tribunals to treat peremptory norms as merely presumptive rather than absolute.

explanations.correct: The passage traces two interlocking problems — the circularity in validating jus cogens norms (paragraph 2) and their contested interaction with lex specialis (paragraph 3) — and concludes that the doctrine, despite its theoretical force, remains 'practically unstable.' B integrates both strands and accurately captures the author's overall evaluative thesis.
explanations.A: Too narrow: the passage's concern is not merely that the Vienna Convention omitted a list, but that deeper validation and interaction problems persist. 'Provoking unnecessary litigation' is also not the author's characterization.
explanations.C: Overstates the positivist critique. The author presents it as one contested position, not a 'convincing demonstration,' and does not endorse it.
explanations.D: A paragraph-level detail masquerading as the main point; the author explicitly says the Court 'offered no satisfactory account,' making D doubly inaccurate.
explanations.E: Too narrow: bilateral investment treaties are one illustration in paragraph 3; the passage's broader concern is the foundational validation problem addressed throughout.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the International Court of Justice's 1998 advisory opinion can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unqualified approval, because the opinion resolved the principal controversy surrounding jus cogens validation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cautious endorsement tempered by acknowledgment that the opinion's practical impact has been limited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partial approval for endorsing the defenders' position on jus cogens, coupled with criticism that the opinion left the underlying theoretical problem unaddressed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutral reportage, since the author presents the opinion without evaluating its adequacy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sharp disapproval, because the opinion aligned the Court with a philosophically untenable natural-law position.

explanations.correct: The author notes the Court 'appeared to endorse the defenders' position' — a tentative approval — but then states the Court 'offered no satisfactory account' of the theoretical problem that motivated the dispute. C captures both the partial approval and the pointed criticism accurately.
explanations.A: Contradicted by the author's explicit statement that the Court provided no satisfactory theoretical account.
explanations.B: Mischaracterizes the criticism: the author's objection is theoretical, not merely about limited practical impact.
explanations.D: The phrase 'offered no satisfactory account' is evaluative, not neutral reportage.
explanations.E: Overstated in both valence and content; the author does not characterize the Court's position as 'philosophically untenable' or invoke natural law as the objection.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and defined; one theoretical objection to the doctrine is presented and then refuted; an unresolved practical dispute involving the doctrine is described; and a proposal for resolving the dispute is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its foundational ambiguity identified; the principal theoretical controversy surrounding the doctrine is examined; a complicating interaction with a competing legal principle is analyzed; and the author concludes that neither judicial nor legislative efforts have resolved the underlying tensions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing international legal principles are introduced; each is analyzed separately on its own terms; the conditions under which one supersedes the other are delineated; and a preferred resolution is endorsed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A treaty provision is described; a series of cases applying that provision are examined in chronological order; the cases are found to be mutually inconsistent; and a reform of the treaty is recommended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A theoretical dispute is introduced; the author endorses one side of the dispute; an illustrative case study is provided; and the endorsed position is shown to be confirmed by the case study.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces jus cogens and identifies the foundational ambiguity (no enumeration of qualifying norms). Paragraph 2 examines the circular-validation controversy between positivists and defenders. Paragraph 3 analyzes the lex specialis complication. Paragraph 4 concludes that neither the ICJ nor the ILC has resolved the tensions. B matches this four-paragraph progression precisely.
explanations.A: Inaccurate: the author does not refute the positivist objection — it is left as a live controversy — and 'a proposal for resolving the dispute' overstates the closing paragraph's tentative hope.
explanations.C: Misrepresents the structure: the passage does not analyze jus cogens and lex specialis 'separately on their own terms' or endorse a preferred resolution.
explanations.D: Fabricates a chronological case-law analysis; the passage does not examine cases in chronological order, and the closing is not a treaty-reform recommendation.
explanations.E: The author does not endorse either side of the positivist/defender dispute, and the lex specialis section does not confirm any endorsed position.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a consequence specified by the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties when a treaty conflicts with a jus cogens norm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The treaty is suspended pending review by a standing international adjudicative body.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The treaty is void from its inception.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The states party to the treaty are required to renegotiate its terms within a prescribed period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The offending provisions of the treaty are severed, leaving the remainder in force.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The treaty is voidable at the election of the state whose rights under the jus cogens norm have been infringed.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that the Vienna Convention 'provides that any treaty conflicting with such a norm is void ab initio' — void from its inception. B is a direct paraphrase of that statement.
explanations.A: No such suspension mechanism is mentioned in the passage; this is a plausible-world fabrication.
explanations.B: Correct: 'void ab initio' means void from the beginning, precisely what B states.
explanations.C: No renegotiation requirement appears in the passage.
explanations.D: Severability of offending provisions is not discussed; the passage says the entire treaty is void.
explanations.E: The passage specifies voidness, not voidability at election — a critical legal distinction the passage does not make.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legal positivism provides a fully adequate framework for understanding why jus cogens norms occupy a superior position in international law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A state that entered into a bilateral investment treaty prior to the establishment of a relevant jus cogens norm may have a legitimate basis for invoking lex specialis before an arbitral tribunal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inability of the International Law Commission's 2019 draft conclusions to resolve the foundational tensions of jus cogens doctrine suggests that a treaty-based solution may be preferable to continued reliance on advisory opinions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the same evidentiary machinery validates both ordinary custom and jus cogens norms, states may freely derogate from peremptory norms by concluding bilateral treaties that supersede them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The concept of obligations erga omnes is entirely distinct from jus cogens and should not be invoked in the same analytical framework.

explanations.correct: The author states in paragraph 4 that neither the ICJ nor the ILC's 2019 draft conclusions have resolved the tensions, and closes by expressing hope for 'a future multilateral treaty' with an enumeration and a standing adjudicative body. This directly supports C's inference that the author regards a treaty-based solution as preferable to continued reliance on advisory opinions.
explanations.A: The author presents the positivist critique as a challenge, not as a complete and adequate framework; the author does not endorse it.
explanations.B: The passage notes arbitral panels are divided and does not suggest any temporal priority argument for bilateral investment treaties; this goes beyond what the passage supports.
explanations.D: This restates the positivist critique in its most extreme form; the author does not endorse the conclusion that derogation is therefore permissible.
explanations.E: The passage treats erga omnes as the characterization the ICJ applied to jus cogens, implying they are related, not distinct.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of arbitral tribunals' divided treatment of lex specialis arguments (third paragraph) serves primarily to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: refute the legal-positivist claim that jus cogens norms are analytically indistinguishable from ordinary customary norms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate that the theoretical ambiguities identified in the second paragraph have concrete, unresolved consequences in institutional legal practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that bilateral investment treaties are generally incompatible with international human rights obligations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide an example of a case in which the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion was directly applied by arbitral tribunals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the lex specialis principle should be eliminated from international law because it consistently undermines peremptory norms.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph moves from the theoretical controversy of paragraph 2 to its real-world manifestation: arbitral panels are actually divided because the underlying doctrine is unsettled. The function is to show that the abstract circularity problem has tangible institutional consequences — that it is not merely a philosophical puzzle but a source of inconsistent adjudication.
explanations.A: The third paragraph does not address the positivist critique at all; it concerns a different doctrinal complication.
explanations.C: The passage does not generalize about human rights obligations; it uses one class of bilateral investment treaty disputes as an illustration.
explanations.D: The passage does not state that the ICJ's 1998 opinion was applied by the arbitral tribunals discussed; in fact, the author implies the tribunals' inconsistency reflects the opinion's inadequacy.
explanations.E: The author does not call for the elimination of lex specialis; the passage treats it as a legitimate competing principle that is difficult to reconcile with jus cogens.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the defenders' response to the positivist critique as that response is described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states whose national legal systems are rooted in civil-law traditions have formally incorporated jus cogens norms into their domestic constitutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: International tribunals have, on multiple occasions, applied jus cogens norms to invalidate bilateral treaties even over the objection of both parties to those treaties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Empirical surveys of state practice reveal that the norms most frequently asserted as jus cogens candidates are accepted by significantly fewer than all states, with several economically powerful states explicitly registering dissent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prohibition on torture has been recognized as a jus cogens norm by every regional human rights tribunal that has considered the question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scholars working in the natural-law tradition have long argued that certain moral norms are so fundamental as to bind states regardless of their consent.

explanations.correct: The defenders respond that peremptory norms reflect a 'near-universal moral consensus so fundamental that no bilateral agreement ought to be capable of abrogating them.' The defenders' response thus depends on the claim of near-universality. If, in fact, the norms asserted as jus cogens candidates are accepted by significantly fewer than all states — with powerful states dissenting — the near-universality premise collapses, and the qualitative distinction from ordinary custom becomes very difficult to sustain.
explanations.A: Strengthens rather than weakens the defenders' position by showing institutional embrace of jus cogens norms.
explanations.B: Also strengthens, demonstrating that the norms operate with the peremptory force defenders claim.
explanations.C: Correct: directly attacks the near-universality premise that anchors the defenders' qualitative distinction.
explanations.D: Strengthens the defenders' view by showing near-universal recognition of at least one specific norm.
explanations.E: Supports the defenders' philosophical underpinnings rather than undermining them, even if it does not directly resolve the positivist's evidentiary challenge.
